subsubtopic: AGENCY AGREEMENT WITH CONSUMERS DISTRIBUTING COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, along with many thousands of Canadian business people, was deeply disturbed by the news reports that Canada Post is entering into an agreement to work hand in hand with Consumers Distributing to act as an active agent for that company. This is indeed unprecedented, unwarranted, and unfair competition for the private sector which has enough problems as it is trying to keep afloat in these difficult times.
If this scheme is allowed to proceed, Canada Post in almost every community in Canada would give Consumers Distributing an unfair advantage and unfair access to all the retail markets without significant community investment and contribution in terms of taxes and employment. Canada Post has all it can do to improve the postal service, and should leave the distribution of consumer goods to those who can do it best, the private sector. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I call upon the Government to take the necessary steps immediately to direct Canada Post to countermand such an agreement with Consumers Distributing and other similar hare-brained schemes which may surface in the future.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of all Canadians and especially on behalf of Quebecers, I want to take this opportunity to pay tribute to our compatriot, Gaetan Boucher. At the Winter Games, Gaetan managed to win three Olympic medals, including one bronze medal for the 500 metres and two gold medals. There has never been any doubt as to Gaetan Boucher's athletic skills since he has been able to compete with athletes of his stature.
Mr. Speaker, I also would like to take this opportunity to praise the efforts of Sport Canada which for a number of years has been helping young Canadian athletes across the country.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that Gaetan Boucher is an inspiration to young Canadians who would all like their country to be proud of them some day. Three cheers for Gaetan Boucher, the world champion!

Mr. Speaker, I understand that it takes an average of 10 months for a veteran to get a ruling from the Canada Pension Commission upon applying for veterans' benefits. This is not acceptable. It is too long for a veteran in distress to have to wait. Add to that the length of time for the Pension Review Board to make a decision and you have a total of 19 months. That is an average amount of time. Many wait much longer. That is more than one and one-half years. I am told that the Bureau of Pensions Advocates takes five and one-half months. Add to this the more than two months that the War Veterans Allowance Board makes them wait, and I maintain that it is unconscionable to make our veterans wait that long for a decision.
I also think, Mr. Speaker, that a more compassionate attitude should be extended to our aging veterans, and much more consideration should be given to their health problems, many of which are due to their being burnt out from direct results of war experiences.

Mr. Speaker, my statement is with respect to Canadair. The Canadian Government is picking up a $3.5 billion debt on behalf of that Crown corporation. That is enough money to double the income supplements of every poor pensioner in the country and have $1 billion left over. This is a staggering sum, Mr. Speaker. Canadair has been staggeringly mismanaged. The new company could also lose money since it has orders for jet engines which it must continue to buy.
The Liberal Government has given Crown corporations a bad name in spite of the fact that there have been successes in

March 14, 1984
Canada with Crown corporations at both federal and provincial levels. We have a mixed economy in Canada. The future role of the Crown corporation is indeed a challenge to the left, as well as being open to obvious criticism from the right.
I advocate three things. The first is that this mismanagement not go unpunished. The second is that Crown corporations be open to public scrutiny. Messrs. Strong, Bell, and Austin are strong individuals but are not really accountable to anyone. There should be a special parliamentary committee for Crown corporations which would have the powers of an American congressional committee. Finally, we should integrate Crown corporation strategies into a national industrial game plan. Then we will not have $3.5 billion spent to produce an executive jet. I find that a strange priority. It is a real blight on Crown corporations in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALL-PARTY SUPPORT REQUESTED FOR IMPROVING THE ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, I was very pleased when I found out that Quebec had finally decided to focus more attention on the North Shore, and I am referring to plans for establishing an aluminum refinery in Sept-Iles. Mr. Speaker, it is very important that Quebec and the federal Government co-operate on this project and ensure that it will come to fruition.
I know that the company concerned has already met federal officials and that the Canadian Government has confirmed and is prepared to take part in the project if it receives a request from the Kaiser Corporation.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that all parties in the House will be able to give their approval very shortly so that we can bring a new industry into the region, in order to put the economy back on the rails, and not only in Sept-Iles but in the entire region, which in addition to Sept-Iles includes Schefferville, Gagnon, Fermont, the people of Port Cartier, and the people on the lower North Shore, who all stand to benefit.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR SUPPLEMENTARY FUNDS FOR YOUNG STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope you will allow me to follow the example of my colleague from Verdun and welcome our famous guest. I want to congratulate him on his outstanding performance which has made all Canadians feel very proud. Mr. Speaker, this is the second time I mention this extraordinary performance.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the Minister responsible for student employment that the Government recently appointed a Minister of Youth. However, to give young people hope for the future, we must have budgets that are commensurate with the number of young people who will be looking for work this summer. As far as the Summer Canada Program is concerned, Mr. Speaker-and I know my colleagues are already aware of this-the interest expressed in it by young people vastly exceeds proposed funding.
Today, I want to urge the Minister to make additional funding available so that these young students will not be disappointed when they start looking for jobs this summer. In the circumstances ... I hear Hon. Members complaining, I am sure I do not know why, Mr. Speaker. On behalf of these young people, I would simply ask the Government to be responsible and compassionate, and to provide additional funding so that this summer, young students will be able to earn a few dollars to help them pay for their education. Mr. Speaker, that was the gist of what I wanted to say today, and I hope my colleagues were listening carefully.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association has recently reported that already in this year, 1984, four new foreign built supply ships have been registered for use in our East Coast offshore operations. Canadian shipyards could have built those vessels, and the benefit to Canada would have been in the order of $55 million. They were not built in Canada because of the availability of cheaper financing abroad, and muddled federal policies here.
Consider the obstacles facing the Canadian shipbuilder. Not only must the builder contend with direct and indirect subsidies offered by foreign competitors, the builder must also face
March 14, 1984

the fact that the Canadian Government, the Government to which he pays taxes, will rebate up to 80 per cent of the importer's leasing costs or customs duty. A shipowner sourcing in Canada is not eligible for any rebate whatsoever. The result in 1983 was a record importation of foreign built vessels to Canada.
If the Government is serious about job creation and the preservation of a viable Canadian shipbuilding industry, let it act now to encourage sourcing in Canada. No industry should have to fight its own Government in the international marketplace.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF SEPARATE MINISTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's No. 1 industry continues to decline and the Liberal Government continues to ignore the problem. Yesterday the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Caccia), the Government's excuse for a Minister of Forestry, said that he was too busy to attend the inaugural luncheon for the Canadian Forest Industries Council.
Much of our traditional forest resource has been depleted. Twenty-five million hectares of logged-over lands have not been adequately restocked. Some of our traditional markets are drying up. Logging and sawmill communities suffer from widespread unemployment and economic insecurity. But the Minister does not have enough time to meet with industry representatives.
Long term forestry agreements have not been signed with the major forestry provinces. In 1984-85 British Columbia has to make do with an $11 million extension of an agreement, instead of a new agreement which would have seen over $100 million provided in federal-provincial funds.
This neglect of our basic industry must stop. As a start, the Government should establish a separate ministry of forestry with a full time minister, not a part time person who is out to lunch whenever forest industry representatives come to call.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT URGED TO GRANT POSTHUMOUS PARDON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, like so many other Canadians, am disappointed at the lack of agreement between the First Ministers and native leaders at the constitutional conference on March 8 and 9. One would suppose that after all the negotiations and study, some agreement could have been reached on the four agenda items under discussion at the conference, namely, equality rights, aboriginal title and rights including treaty rights, land and resources,
Oral Questions
and self-government. Because of the failure, the federal Government should initiate action on its own to spur the provinces into addressing aboriginal issues in a more substantive way.
The federal Government deserves support for its March 9 announcement on removal of sexual discrimination from the Indian Act.
It is hoped and anticipated that provincial Governments during their annual premiers' conference will place native issues at the top of their agenda.
In addition, it would be appropriate for the federal Government to move to correct an historic injustice by granting a posthumous pardon to Louis Riel. The Government could proceed on this matter through a Bill I introduced in the last session, and which I will be reintroducing again, I hope today.

subsubtopic: CANADAIR-GOVERNMENT'S PARTICIPATION IN CHALLENGER AIRCRAFT CONSTRUCTION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board. He will know from his experience in this House that Members of this Party have questioned the Government's decision to be involved in the Challenger program, since 1976. In the 1982 Shielding Report, which the Government commissioned, we find:
-the business of selling executive aircraft is undisciplined, ruthless, and checkered by practices which any government should abhor.
Why does the Government continue to damage the job opportunities and the future of those working for Canadair by insisting on carrying on in a business checkered by practices that any Government should abhor?

your act together and come up with a policy. We know that your Leader is unable to spell out his policies, but if some Members of the Opposition do have policies and ideas, they ought to combine their efforts and suggest a few policies which their Leader might follow.

Member wants to destroy not only the Challenger Program, but Canadair and the thousands of jobs there, as well as the thousands of jobs in the hands of sub-contractors, he can argue that, but he will be rejected on this by the Canadian people, as his Party was in the last election when it wanted to do something similar with Petro-Canada.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, there are certain people in this House who want a Crown corporation to be running, but they want it to be running efficiently, in the interest of the workers directly affected, and in the interest of the taxpayers of Canada. The $2 billion plus bailout is ten times the amount of money the Government is prepared to allocate in new funds for youth employment this year. It is fully equivalent to all the money set aside for job training and job creation for the total number of unemployed, in the Budget this year. What conditions has the Government laid down in terms of the performance of Canadair to give the workers directly affected in Montreal, and the rest of the people in Canada, reason to believe that that company is now a viable entity?

ly viable elements and a marketing potential which will allow us not only to protect existing jobs, but also to use innovative technology so that these jobs will still be there in 10 years from now and will have expanded.

subtopic: CORPORATION'S MANAGEMENT-ACCOUNTABILITY FOR EXPENDITURE OF PUBLIC MONEY
CORPORATION'S MANAGEMENT-ACCOUNTABILITY FOR EXPENDITURE OF PUBLIC MONEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked the question I did because the only answer that was given in the committee yesterday by the Senator responsible was in terms of trying to convey the impression that we should have greater confidence because, by splitting the company and the people of Canada absorbing the debt at an atrociously high cost, potential customers for this airplane would know that the company is in a more financially viable position. Potential customers always knew that a Crown corporation backed by the taxpayers of Canada was in that position. Nothing has changed.
Given the past record of very incompetent management that misled the Government, telling it that the company had ten times the number of orders for the aircraft than it actually had at one time, will the Minister tell us why we should have a greater degree of confidence in the existing management of Canadair? Also, what procedures does the Government to implement to give a greater degree of ongoing accountability for this spending of public money?

concerns the first part of the Hon. Concerning the last part of the question, which dealt with how these companies could be made more accountable to Parliament, I believe that the fact that the CDIC and Canadair, de Havilland, or other corporations regularly appear before Standing Committees as they are now doing, is an indication that there already is an appropriate mechanism to ensure that these companies are held accountable to Parlia-

ment for their management. Furthermore, a Bill is soon to be introduced in the House to authorize the changes made to CDIC and related corporations. This Bill will also introduce amendments which will enable the House to hold these corporations accountable to a greater extent for their management.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister knows that up to this point none of the procedures have been changed in terms of the accountability of this Crown corporation or of any other Crown corporation. subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I concluded my remarks yesterday I was pointing out that John Turner had set the course for the Government's continued deficit financing. Since then Canadians have learned that such deficits are not cure-alls. The Ontario Economic Council points out very forcibly that such huge deficits crowd out desirable investments. When the federal Government borrows 90 cents of every dollar put aside by Canadians, it starts a strong competition for the remaining 10 per cent. The higher interest rates, which automatically follow on supply and demand, lead to increased inflation. We as a people have gone through that cycle once before. We do not want to do it again, Mr. Speaker, nor can this economic recovery about which we are hearing stand a further round of high interest and inflation.
These high deficits are a reflection of over-spending. Federal government spending for the upcoming fiscal year will exceed $98 billion. This represents a year over year increase of 10.5 per cent. The Minister followed the six and five program of restraint, so he says, by promising to hold the line at 4 per cent in his February Budget. It takes a rather elastic line indeed, one that has lost all of its strength and control, to allow a stretch from 4 per cent to 10.5 per cent.
Bill C-21 is the inevitable result of a government's refusal to live within its means. Every home owner in this country knows how discouraging it is to pay on a mortgage year after year and not see any reduction on the principal of that mortgage. When individual citizens or organizations borrow money and go into debt, they must repay their loans as well as interest that has accumulated on it. Governments are really no different, except that some governments close their eyes and increase taxation. It is that simple for them. But tell that to the taxpayers of St. Catharines. They know what a thousand dollars is worth. They believe that their tax dollar is going into Public Works, National Defence, social programs and so on. But not any more. That $1,000 per taxpayer in St. Catharines is his annual contribution to the public debt service charges.
It takes no great intellectual wizard to understand that these service charges will crowd essential programs. We want the Government's spending madness to stop now.
To put it quite simply, I would be treating the taxpayers in my riding with contempt if 1 voted for this legislation. It is

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-21, an Act to provide borrowing authority, asks Members of Parliament to give the federal Government approval to borrow $29.55 billion for fiscal year 1984-85. How can responsible Members of Parliament possibly give blanket approval to such an amount and to such an unspecified request? Why does the Government not indicate which budgetary items this is to cover? How can we approve expenditures which we believe, in the most part, are unnecessary or wrong?
We in this Party do not agree that the Government should have given over $1.35 billion to Canadair. Now it plans to wipe out this debt completely and provide a further loan of $310 million. We did not agree with the PIP grants to oil companies which cost over $1.6 billion. We did not and do not approve the borrowing of moneys for Liberal patronage and slush funds, nor do we approve of the deferral of corporate taxes which could bring $22 billion more into this year's Budget and thus require much less borrowing authority. We do not agree with the loss of taxes from unnecessary loopholes which the Government is only too glad to give to high-paid professionals and high-income people in its latest Budget.
I oppose this Bill for the same reasons that I opposed the Liberal Budget which included unnecessary costs, which forgot the hundreds of thousands of unemployed people, which made only a token grant for youth jobs and completely ignored jobs
Borrowing Authority Act
and training for women. It gave all the benefits to higher-income people and corporations. This is just another Tory type of financing; it is not humanitarian or practical.
In particular, the federal Budget was not a love story for Canadian women. Canadian women are struggling as never before to survive and pay their costs. In many cases they are the sole supporters of their families. The Budget contained the long-awaited increase in the GIS for poor single pensioners. Of course, we would agree with borrowing money for that, but we must point out that it was long overdue and certainly is not enough to bring pensioners above the poverty line. Unfortunately, it leaves elderly single women who make up three-quarters of this group well below the poverty line. The average income of pensioners with no other income will rise to only $7,200. This amount is $624 short of the minimum amount recommended by the all-Party task force on pension reform. It is much below the real poverty line.
We agree with pension splitting between spouses proposed in the Budget. It is another program which was long advocated by women's organizations. It does not cost the Government a cent. Why did it not bring in this policy sooner? However, our major concerns regarding pension reform are that the Liberals, like the Conservatives, concentrate only on private pension schemes. There is no way that this will provide adequate, secure retirement coverage for the needs of Canadian women in particular. The Liberals refuse to reform the public pension plan even though the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) advocated this in earlier speeches. We know that this is the only way to ensure adequate universal pension coverage for all retired people. Canada Pension Plan benefits should have been increased to 50 per cent of the average industrial wage.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare stated in her Budget speech that the Budget brought in "ideal pensions". Then, of course, she had to admit that it depended entirely upon how the private sector responded and to say that this was its last chance. Obviously she is not completely confident that the Liberal pension proposals will be taken up by the private sector. The Liberal pension plan is based upon tax deductions and voluntary individual payments into RRSPs.

How many businesses will be able to find the extra cash flow to put in place schemes for their employees, even though they may be a little broader in proposed coverage?

Mr. Speaker, I must say that the time allotment ran out for the last speaker at the most appropriate moment. She was ready to make sure that the rich get more out of the Treasury and deprive the poor.
In speaking to this borrowing Bill, there is a sense of dej'a vu. We are back to the same thing again. In the four years in the life of this Parliament, this is the eighth borrowing request. That is in addition to the regular revenues that the Government receives. Within the life of this Parliament we are looking at a cumulative borrowing of S 102.85 billion, almost $103 billion. I agree with the other Members that it is bad enough to have such things as the bailout of Maislin and Canadair and some other projects, but I object if much of this borrowing is, as it probably is, to help with the Liberal slush fund. In the last month or two, we have repeatedly heard about special funds provided for Liberal back-benchers only. They have total discretion over how those funds are spent in their constituencies, and maybe in others.
To get a picture of what is going on in the whole scene of borrowing in this country, we have to put it in perspective with past experience. In this one Bill, we are asked to give the Government permission to borrow $29.55 billion. In this one borrowing authority, they are asking for almost three times as much as the total deficit of the entire nation in all of Canadian history when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came into office in 1968. Our country was in debt for $11 billion for the First 101 years of our history. In one borrowing authority, we are being asked to give permission to borrow almost three times that amount for one year.

Member for Restigouche. What kind of unnecessary interruptions could there be during the next year? Could there be such things as a leadership race in the Liberal Party? Would that be an unnecessary interruption? Following the leadership convention in June, would a possible general election be an unnecessary interruption?
What does the Member mean by "unnecessary interruption"? Does he mean that an interruption is the need to come back to Parliament to borrow more money? In two of the eight borrowing Bills in the last four years we discovered that the Government was asking for far more money than it needed to operate. The Government had to reduce the amount requested in Bill C-125, at the request of the Opposition. It reduced by $4 billion the amount in Bill C-151 because Opposition Members demanded it. The Government was borrowing more than it needed so that it would not have to keep coming back to Parliament for more money. It is a nuisance factor in this parliamentary system for the Government to come back to
March 14, 1984

Parliament and ask for more money. It is a subtle reminder that it is overspending.
The Hon. Member for Restigouche talked about avoiding unnecessary interruption. It is another way of saying that the Government is asking for permission to borrow more than it needs, as it does not want to come back to Parliament to ask for permission at very awkward moments. Those awkward moments happen to be such things as leadership conventions and election campaigns. Between now and March 31, 1985, the Government will have permission to borrow enough money so that it will not have to put up with the nuisance of coming back to Parliament. I do not think that we as Members can afford to see this institution as being a nuisance or an unnecessary interruption for the Government. This is the arena in which the Government must display what little sense of responsibility it has left.
As I said before, if in fact there were no such things as Liberal slush funds or bailouts and the Government still needed all of this money, then there would be another very serious question to ask, and that is, whether we are living within our means. Are we paring down the Budget in such a way that we can operate using our cash flow? When this particular borrowing Bill will amount to 4.5 per cent of our GNP or cash flow, we must ask ourselves whether the Government is prepared to live within the means at its disposal.
I noticed that under this particular borrowing Bill, interest payments alone will cost every taxpayer $1,500 a year. That is needed just to meet the interest payments. That, Mr. Speaker, is like going to Household Finance to pay for your grocery bill. They want a little more every time, and we cannot afford to pay those kinds of interest rates. Mr. Speaker, on most occasions it is a pleasure to rise in the House, but it is not a pleasure when discussing a borrowing Bill of the size of the one that is before us at this time. One might recall that in 1969, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that we will be on the road to financial disaster if nothing is done to bring spending under control. In that year, we spent $13.8 billion. Now we are spending $100 billion a year and we can see the problems that that has created.
It is interesting to look over the records and see just who was in charge of our public accounts and spending programs in the past. I have a list here which goes back to 1967 when Mr. Benson was the Minister of Finance. Something that should stand him in good stead, I suppose, as he continues in government service for what seems to be a very long time is that he was the last Finance Minister for the Liberal Government who in 1969-70 showed a surplus. He actually showed a surplus of $493 million in 1969. That was the last surplus the Government ever had, and that was 15 years ago or more. The original idea behind accounting in a businesslike way was that one would lose some money one year and save it up the next.
In 1970, Mr. Benson lost $372 million, and the following year the deficit reached $702 million. In those days that seemed to be pretty horrible. The deficit rose to just under a billion dollars in what would appear to be Mr. Benson's final year as Minister of Finance.
Next, the Hon. John Turner came on to the scene in 1972 and began to lead the way. He produced a 1972-73 Budget which lost $999 million. He produced a Budget in 1974 which lost $1,733 million on the year's operations, and then he produced another Budget in 1975 which nearly quadrupled

March 14, 1984

that loss, making a deficit of $5,463 million. At that point, the Elon. John Turner withdrew from public life in shame and humiliation, one might assume, or to protect himself from having the reputation of being a member of the Liberal Party. However, in any case, he disappeared, and I believe he is now being resurrected as the only hope for leader of the Liberal Party and his coronation is to take place in June of this year.
I would like to let it be known that the record of the Hon. John Turner shows that in the first year he took over, he lost about a billion dollars, and in the last year that he was in charge of our financial operations, the deficit was $5 billion. By that time, the gross debt had risen to $58 billion from some $45 billion, which was the amount of the debt when he took over.

In the year following that in which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was Minister of Finance, the deficit dropped from $12.2 billion to $11.4 billion. That is when the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) was Minister of Finance. John Turner, although some people class the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources as being on a par with Mr. Turner. that Party. It is an interesting commentary on the Government that when the Prime Minister announced his resignation, the stock market went up immediately. There are a lot of examples of this Government's misadventures and its waste of money, Mr. Speaker. As was stated by Decima Research just the other day, people in Canada would like somebody to be the Prime Minister who can sympathize with or understand their problems. That has been a big problem for the Prime Minister, and I am afraid it will be for his successor.

Many of us here have seen that sort of thing take place in this country in the 1950s and 1960s. We do not particularly want that to happen again, but it is more than puzzling to think of the odd sense of priorities the Government must have when it devotes $1 billion, $2 billion or more to the future of a single corporation which employs some 7,000 to
8.000	people, while that same Government, when faced with the crying need for investment in an industry, such as the forest industry which contributes more than the next five industries put together to the Canadian economy, watches that industry starve and the resource disappear. Does the average Canadian know what is a billion dollars? It is a thousand million dollars. It is a stack of brand-new $1 bills piled 85 miles high. That is what we are doing now. This Government comes to us with all kinds of plans and programs. A couple of years ago it came in with the six and five program which was to restrain federal spending. There would no longer be the need to come back every year and pile on the deficit. Incidentally, the gross debt in 1983 was $159 billion. We are adding roughly $30 billion, which will make it $190 billion. Budgetary forecasts will pile another $110 billion on to this accumulated deficit over the next four years.
Are you surprised, Mr. Speaker, that we are upset? Are you surprised that we say we will stand here until there is not a breath left on this side of the House before we give the Government the authority to spend that kind of money? The Minister says there was overtime which the public servants had to work that was not calculated in the six and five program. In addition, the Government was obliged to pay some back pay. Of course, there were some promotions, as well as the normal increments that come with length of service.

What is the excuse here? The excuse is that this Government spends 25 cents of every dollar it takes in on interest payments. subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been presented with yet another borrowing authority Bill, the eighth since 1980, and the largest ever, surpassing the next highest one, Bill C-143, by $10.55 billion. We are not surprised, given the projected deficit for 1984-85 of $29.6 billion, that the Government has come before this House to ask for the authority to borrow in order to cover that deficit of $29.55 billion, of which $4 billion in authority is a cushion above and beyond the $25.5 billion which the Government in its Budget says it requires at this time.
The Budget anticipates a deficit of $29.6 billion. The Government has non-budgetary sources for $4.05 billion. It needs $25.5 billion to cover a deficit which, in itself, is far too large. That $29.55 billion in borrowing authority would allow the deficit to grow to $33.5 billion.
We are not surprised over this Bill, given the inability of this Government to control its expenditures. But we are alarmed. We are alarmed because of what this Bill represents-the deficit of $29.5 billion and the authority to allow that deficit to be $4 billion more than expected. My colleagues have strongly criticized this Bill, and for good reason. I wish to add my criticisms, but not only for the $4 billion contingency fund. More important, I am criticizing the assumptions which underlie a request for the support by this House of continued
Borrowing Authority Act
massive government expenditure and, as a result, an intolerably massive government deficit.
That is what we are being asked to support. We are being asked to agree to the proposed deficit for this coming year. Because we are being asked to borrow to support its expected deficit, we are actually being asked to support a potential of $33.5 billion for 1984-85, $2 billion more than last year's deficit. I share my colleagues' concern over this request to borrow over $29.5 billion. I share their concern for any request above $15 billion because, simply put, this Government proposes to spend too much. The Government is living far beyond its means.
I would like to discuss several aspects of basic economics of which the Government appears to be unaware. I refer to the high economic costs of supporting a large and growing deficit. To support a large deficit, a too large deficit such as that which we have been experiencing for years, the Government has two choices, both of which will continue to harm an already slowing economy. It can borrow on capital markets and it can borrow its $29.55 billion from those markets. However, borrowing as large a percentage of available Canadian funds as the Government is asking for today will crowd out productive private sector borrowing which, by the simple law of supply and demand, will raise interest rates.
The projected deficit for 1984-85 is equal to 91 per cent of expected personal savings. What will happen? Interest rates will be forced to rise as they have already begun to. Through borrowing an additional $29.5 billion on capital markets interest rates will rise further, which will have the result of further slowing the growth which we could otherwise have hoped for.
Productivity and growth in the country are at a lower rate than a country of Canada's wealth and resources should have to put up with. Our productivity is the lowest in the industrialized world. Unlike what we have heard from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), our potential for growth over the next year is not great. According to both Statistics Canada and the Conference Board of Canada, growth is slowing. An increased government deficit will not help this situation.
The business community to which the Government is now turning for stimulation of the economy cannot achieve its potential in a shrinking money market. It cannot achieve its potential in the current economic environment. Canadians are now afraid to take the risks which are fundamental to increased productivity. If the Government crowds the capital markets further, business investment which dropped 12.2 per cent in 1983 will continue to decline.
We all know what happens when the Government borrows heavily. Interest rates will rise and Canadian investors will be forced to borrow abroad, which will increase our foreign debt, productivity will decline further and unemployment will rise. We have seen this happen in the very recent past, Mr. Speaker, and we will not stand by and watch history repeat itself.

March 14, 1984
Borrowing Authority Act
The Globe and Mail carried an article this past Saturday discussing the desperate need for equity capital in Canada. The Government, by maintaining its spending patterns, is robbing business of a chance to raise money for expansion and productive development. Any rise in interest rates will further threaten an already serious situation in which corporations desperately need capital for growth.
Because of the Government's insistence on spending beyond its means and borrowing on capital markets, interest rates will rise, thus denying business the ability to amass its well needed equity. I refer particularly to small businessmen and farmers. We certainly know that the small business and farming sectors are the backbone of the nation. Denying the small business sector the financing it needs at affordable rates will have a definite effect on unemployment. Farmers will be forced to renew mortgages in order to meet capital expenditures and operating expenses. The farmers will not be able to repay these mortgages because we know that interest rates are intolerable at the present time and that we cannot expect to see zero growth in interest rates in the future. We are denying the equity small businessmen and farmers need in order to be productive.
There is another choice for the Government to make which has equally negative effects. The Bank of Canada could simply be given the licence to print money to fund the borrowing requirements of a spendthrift government. The Bank of Canada has created a total of $12 billion for that purpose in the past 12 years. What happens if the Bank of Canada continues to print money? Inflation rises once again.
During the past recession, Canadians have paid dearly for the Government's mismanagement of the economy. We have suffered high rates of inflation because the Government refuses to take responsibility for the economy. If it turns to the Bank of Canada one more time, Canadians will be subjected to another recession like the one from which we are apparently emerging.
There is yet another choice for the Government to make, Mr. Speaker, and it is the only real choice which will not ruin the economy. The Government must do one of two things. It must begin to take the necessary measures to decrease its spending, it must attack its deficit seriously by examining expenditures to see which are unnecessary or wasteful and it must have the guts to priorize spending and cut out those expenditures which do nothing more than increase the deficit. However, if the Government cannot take that fundamental and central step, it must allow another government to do so.
I agree with my colleagues who have stated that it would be irresponsible at best for the House, which represents the people of Canada, to pass this Bill. Simply put, the costs are much too high.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in the debate on Bill C-21, the borrowing authority Bill, but I am less than pleased that the federal Government is making the request. I am particularly concerned about the magnitude of the borrowing request for $29.55 billion. That is a tremendous amount of money and it is difficult to understand it in average terms today. I would not be so concerned if I thought the borrowing would be beneficial to the people of Canada or the people of the riding that I represent, but that will not be the case.

March 14, 1984
Borrowing Authority Act
The deficit lies heavily on the Canadian economy. I have seen many personal tragedies since 1980 which are the result of failed businesses, consumer bankruptcies and unemployment. The terrible magnitude of the request demonstrates a government that is out of control, particularly when one considers that the Budget of February 15 said that the borrowing needs of the Government would be $25.5 billion. Less than two days later the Government introduced this Bill requesting $29.55 billion. For the people of Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington, whose concerns I carry with me, this is the equivalent of spending $19,640 in one year for someone with an income of $13,740. The worst part about borrowing the $5,900 to make up the difference is that $3,900 of that $5,900 is money borrowed to pay interest on a previous debt. The total debt in this hypothetical case increases to $36,000 from $30,000. The average Canadian could never carry on his personal financial affairs in this slipshod fashion.
I stated earlier that I would not be so alarmed if I thought all this tremendous borrowing would be of some benefit to Canadians. However, I do not believe this is the case. It has been demonstrated that the $2.4 billion Special Employment Initiatives Program is nothing more than a re-election pork-barrel for the Government. I find it morally reprehensible that the federal Government should discriminate against the unemployed on the basis of where they live. For a government which states it believes in universality of social programs, this exposes its so-called concern for the fraud it really is.
In the northern area of my riding the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) deliberately underestimated unemployment in order to deny individuals access to programs which they paid into and are entitled to. Recently a number of municipalities in that area made representations to the Minister and sent him copies of resolutions they had passed regarding the UIC. Part of the Minister's reply says:
The report I have received from officials of the Commission indicates that the unemployment rate has decreased from mid-October of 1983 to such an extent.. . that the exemption for repeater claimants has no longer been applicable.
He then quoted an unemployment rate of 9.1 per cent. He dismissed any variations in the unemployment rate in a region as a problem of "statistics", was "unclear" about what to do and said that it was "premature" to respond to this very real and pressing problem.
The Minister may be unclear as to the actual rate of unemployment, but officials in his Department are not. Figures supplied to me by his senior officials, in writing, give a community rate of 30 per cent and an area district rate of 21 per cent. A simple check I had done by the Department, which the Minister is equally capable of doing, indicated the number of individuals in an area drawing unemployment insurance. The latest figures indicate that Bancroft, with a population of 2,305 people, has 475 people drawing UI benefits. That is 20.6 per cent unemployment before school children, senior citizens or home makers are included to determine the actual size of the labour force in a village that size. If there was some
indication that the tremendous amount of cash the Government wishes to borrow would go to help these average Canadians, which I do not believe it will, I would Find this Bill less objectionable.
What does the federal Government accomplish by doing this to Canadians? Many constituents ask me this. First, by purposely underestimating the unemployment rate, it tries to make the situation look much better than it really is. Secondly, when the so-called rate of unemployment drops to 11.5 per cent, the repeater clause in the Unemployment Insurance Act is no longer applicable. This results in a lower pay-out by the federal Government. It disqualifies individuals who normally should qualify for UI benefits. The Government shifts the burden to the financially pressed local municipalities by inflating their welfare rolls, creating a further hardship on local residents as property taxes rise to meet these obligations. Finally, the area concerned is denied fair access to employment programs such as Canada Works, LEAD, and the Special Employment Initiatives Program, all of which are based on the rate of unemployment.
I believe the Government should be searching for ways to reduce the deficit instead of deliberately underestimating the deficit each time it presents its forecast. The forecast of declining deficits must become a reality if this country is going to sustain a prolonged and lasting recovery into the next century. It is also clear that the negative impact of this huge deficit will adversely affect small business, the number one job creator in this country. The federal Government should be helping small business, not hurting it.
It was appalled by the news that Canada Post is entering the catalogue shopping business by processing orders for Consumers Distributing Limited. There is no demonstrated need for this service and it is blatantly unfair competition. Canada Post should concentrate on improving its level of service before trying something new. The individuals who operate the shops and stores in our local communities have put a lot of time, effort and investment into their business and community. Their taxes subsidize the losses of Canada Post. Now they are being called upon to subsidize competition against their business as well.
How the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) or the Minister of Employment and Immigration can say they support free enterprise, entrepreneurialism and the little guy is beyond me. Actions speak louder than words. The present Government's socialism is alive and well in all these pretenders to the Prime Minister's job. Bill C-21 is the latest exercise in fiscal insolvency. I for one do not think we need another $29.5 billion at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I hesitated before deciding whether or not I should reply to all this utter nonsense from the Official Opposition. If we want Canadian men and women who read Hansard or watch proceedings on their TV sets to understand what is really going on in this country in the area of financial and economic
March 14, 1984

management, I feel compelled, as a member of this House, to disprove some of the false statements which we have heard this past hour in the House.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians must decide for themselves whether members of the Opposition are dishonest or uninformed in financial and economic matters, or jokers or more inclined to demagoguery as weeks and months go by. 1 leave them to decide that for themselves. I suggest to them, however, that the truth is really a mixture of everything I have just mentioned.
Mr. Speaker, the Opposition condemns the Government for its considerable deficit and, like outraged women, accuses the Government of wasting public funds and squandering taxpayers' money. In my opinion, there are not a great many ways to reduce a deficit: you either have to increase the tax burden or to cut the spending or both. There is no other way, Mr. Speaker.
Well, let us see what our hon. friends opposite have to offer in standing committees during question periods in the House or debates such as this one. First, in the area of spending.
The new Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) has said several times that the Government of Canada is behaving in a shameful manner towards the Canadian Armed Forces, that we are not respecting our commitments to NATO and that the day his party will form the Government, the budget for the Department of Defence will be substantially increased. This is one area where expenditures will increase.
In addition, what did we hear during the debate on second reading and committee stages of Bill C-3, which is still before the Committee? We were told that, if the federal Government could not agree with the Provinces on the issue of health care, it was not because of extra billing or user fees, but basically because of a question of money, and that when the Progressive Conservative Party takes over, the needs of the provinces will be met and transfer payments will be increased in such a way that the Provinces will have the financial resources they need to provide better health care for the public and higher incomes for the doctors. There would therefore be an increase in expenditures for defence and health care. These budgetary items are very important; I am not suggesting a few hundred thousand dollars or something like ten or twenty million dollars. Those are some of the most important budgetary items to be provided for by the Canadian Government.
I have another example, Mr. Speaker. In recent weeks, the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs has been considering Bill C-17, which is, I believe, the Bill dealing with fiscal transfers for post-secondary education. In June 1982, the Government decided that the transfers would be restricted to a 6 per cent increase in 1983-84 and a 5 per cent increase in 1984-85. What was the Opposition Members'
Borrowing Authority Act
position in the Standing Committee? On this issue, the Government has been accused of smothering post-graduate education at a time when the need is so great. They have also said that, when they are elected, or if they were already in Government at that time, they would be a lot more generous with the Provinces which could then afford to provide much larger amounts of money to community colleges and universities all across Canada. They would increase expenditures, Mr. Speaker. They are not suggesting that they would reduce them.
I have yet another example, Mr. Speaker, which involves research and development, and Heaven knows that we have to make considerable efforts in this area and that we are all aware of it. However, if the Progressive Conservative Party were in power, as they have promised time and time again, the Government effort in this area would be even more important. There would be grants for businesses; there would be tax concessions and tax credits, and this means a further loss of revenue for the Government, Mr. Speaker.
On the one hand, they are asking for more expenditures, and on the other hand, they want to cut the federal Government's revenue. Opposition Members are always claiming that federal taxes are crushing the taxpayer and small and medium-sized businesses. Mr. Speaker, it is time Opposition Members woke up. Of course, the Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) said the other day that they were not going to tell us outright what they would do if they were in power. They would not dare but they just might close down Canadair and put 5,000 or 6,000 people in the Montreal area out of work. They have all kinds of answers, but with the electorate, you have to put your best foot forward. You have to woo the voters. You cannot catch flies with vinegar, Mr. Speaker, you have to use honey. And that is the position of the Opposition Parties and especially the Progressive Conservative Party.
Mr. Speaker, it is too bad that they do not understand what a deficit is ... If you were kind enough to listen, my friends, you might learn something. They do not understand that a deficit is a tool used to apply an economic policy. A government is not managed like a household or a personal budget, because the Government has a responsibility of its own. You know why the budget deficit has suddenly gone up from $9 or $10 billion to $29 or $30 billion, Mr. Speaker? It is quite simple. It is not because the government has recklessly increased its expenditures. Some 70 per cent of the increased budget deficit is due to a drop in government revenues. Another 30 per cent is due to the fact that the recession has saddled the Government with new responsibilities and expenditures, for instance in the unemployment insurance sector.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like the members opposite to tell us specifically which expenditures they would cut, what taxes they would increase and then we could discuss things in an informed and responsible manner without the demagoguery that constantly prevails in the House when the Hon. Members opposite take the floor.

March 14, 1984
Borrowing Authority Act

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member who just spoke for making the best of a very bad situation. The Member spoke about vinegar and honey. The vinegar to which he was referring is very much the record of this administration, which has unfortunately provided a very sour taste for Canadians to contend with for all but a few months in the many years since 1968 when the present Government came to power. The honey which he spoke of I am sure will come in the not too distant future when, as we hope and trust, the Government will screw up its courage and take the issue which is before the House to the people of Canada. We look forward to the opportunity to provide the people of Canada with necessary alternatives.
The Hon. Member also spent a great deal of time looking to the future and speculating on the type of policies a new Conservative Government would bring to the people of Canada. I think he spoke with great foresight. I am sure he is aware, as are the backbenchers on that side of the House, of what the future holds for them. We applaud the Member for his foresight. We hope that the future which he foresees for the country will soon come to be.
However, I would like to deal with the history of that administration as well as the borrowing Bill which is before us, because that is the reality of the moment. As we know and as has been said in the House this afternoon, we have before us the largest borrowing Bill in the history of Canada. It is a Bill that would require Canadians in the future to pay $29.55 billion.
Shortly after the Hon. Member preceding me began to speak, I noticed that some young people sitting in the galleries across from me, members of the Boy Scout organization, left the House. It was unfortunate because it is young people such as them who in the future will have to bear the brunt of the Government's spending policies. In fact, if those young people are aware of what their share of the debt is, they must realize that they owe $7,000 or more. Every person who is born in this country in the days, months and years to come will owe $7,000 or more as a matter of birthright. The longer the Government remains in office, the greater their birthright will become.
As we know, the record of the present Government headed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been one of irresponsible spending. When the Prime Minister and his Government first came to office in 1968 it was spending approximately $12 billion per year. Presently, if one includes what we anticipate to be in the supplementary estimates, it appears that it will be spending $100 billion per year.
The deficit in 1968 was approximately $491 million. We must remember that the Government's estimates have been far from accurate in the past, but it estimates that in the 1984-85 fiscal year the deficit will be $29.6 billion. The harsh reality of the situation is that it may in fact be larger than that.
Of course, the national debt has grown astronomically during the time in which the Prime Minister has been in office
and his Party has been in power. In 1968, the national debt totalled approximately $30 billion. By the end of this fiscal year it will be somewhere in the vicinity of $180 billion to $190 billion. Again, this represents more than $7,000 per man, woman and child.
Unfortunately, the results of this have been largely negative. We wish that they had been otherwise. As a result of the national debt growing at such an astronomical rate, we have seen interest rates rise in the past and we note with concern that it appears they are beginning to rise again. That means, of course, that even the forecast which was presented to us some time ago may be inaccurate because the cost to the Government for its borrowings will be greater than it has anticipated.
It also means that others who would borrow money in the market, such as provincial and municipal governments, businessmen, farmers and others who would use money in order to secure growth, are finding, first, that money is more expensive to borrow than it should be and, second, that they must go outside Canada in order to obtain the money they need. This means that interest dollars which those provincial and municipal governments pay and which people in the private sector pay are often going outside the country as well. Obviously this is a loss to Canada and Canadians.
Consequently, we are spending an incredible amount simply to service the debt which we have before us. In fact, when taxpayers complete their returns at the end of April of this year and send their contributions to the Department of National Revenue, they will sadly realize that $1 out of every $3 they are paying is going simply to pay the debt on moneys already expended. In that sense they feel a tremendous sense of futility and frustration. They are prepared to pay their appropriate share but they believe in many ways that their opportunity to secure growth has been negated by the policies of this administration in the past.
The impact on the average Canadian, the small businessman and the farmers in my constituency is unfortunately very detrimental. First, they find it very difficult to approach their own economic enterprises with confidence because they do not feel that our country is being led in a businesslike manner. They also find it very difficult to borrow money at a reasonable rate of interest. In fact, I could not help but think today of the number of farmers in my constituency who have been forced into bankruptcy in the last few months and those many others who will either be forced into bankruptcy in the months to come or perhaps leave farming because of their inability to carry on. I was thinking of how pleased they would be to have some of their debts eradicated in the manner in which the Government has dealt with Canadair. However, that is another issue.
The problem facing us now is the capacity of this administration to lead this country and the fact that its failure to provide businesslike leadership has meant that there is a lack of confidence in the country, a lack of confidence in the Government and therefore, to a very substantial degree, a lack of confidence in our economy.
March 14, 1984

There are certain times in history when deficit financing is a suitable strategy. The difficulty with what this administration has done is that it has engaged in Keynesian economics, if that is the term one wishes to imply, since the early 1970s. In fact, I suggest it is fair to say that it began to indulge in this strategy during the days of John "Deficit" Turner, who was Minister of Finance from January 28, 1972 until September 9, 1975. During those years the federal deficit in the first year of administration went from $702 million to a grand total of $5,463 billion in the last fiscal year in which he had responsibility.

My colleague refers to the Turner turnpike. Unfortunately, it is a road down which this country has been led in the past at a very high cost to the people of Canada and to the country as a whole. As a result of that indulgence, the Government lost the capacity to be flexible. It lost the capacity to deal with the economic fluctuations of the moment. Therefore, when it finds itself in the present situation of unacceptably high youth unemployment in the vicinity of 20 per cent, and in a situation where their own projections are for 10 per cent unemployment into the foreseeable future, it has lost the capacity to devise new policies to meet that particular crisis.
Borrowing Authority Act
Lately there has been a great deal of emphasis on the subject of newness. Unfortunately, it seems to me that the Government, by virtue of its spendthrift and irresponsible policies in the past, no longer has the capacity or flexibility to provide us with those new policies which the country so desperately needs. Therefore, the only thing we can see in the future that gives us a ray of hope is an election, when it comes in August, October or November. We will be ready when it is called. We will welcome the opportunity to provide the country with the type of businesslike administration which it so desperately needs. We will provide the country with a new government that Canadians will welcome with open arms.
